claim: Vsx genes have a dual role in retina development: an early function in progenitors' specification, and a later requirement for bipolar-cells fate determination in humans and mice.
source: Genetic studies in human and mice have established a dual role for Vsx genes in retina development: an early function in progenitors' specification, and a later requirement for bipolar-cells fate determination.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research in humans and mice.

claim: Mutant models for Vsx genes are available only in mammals.
source: Despite their conserved expression patterns, it is currently unclear to which extent Vsx functions are also conserved across vertebrates, as mutant models are available only in mammals.
evidence: Stated as background knowledge about the state of research.

claim: vsx1 and vsx2 CRISPR/Cas9 double knockouts (vsxKO) in zebrafish show severe visual impairment.
source: Our electrophysiological and histological analyses indicate severe visual impairment and bipolar cells depletion in vsxKO larvae, with retinal precursors being rerouted toward photoreceptor or Müller glia fates.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological and histological data presented in the manuscript.

claim: vsxKO zebrafish larvae show bipolar cells depletion.
source: Our electrophysiological and histological analyses indicate severe visual impairment and bipolar cells depletion in vsxKO larvae, with retinal precursors being rerouted toward photoreceptor or Müller glia fates.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological and histological data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In vsxKO zebrafish, retinal precursors are rerouted toward photoreceptor or Müller glia fates.
source: Our electrophysiological and histological analyses indicate severe visual impairment and bipolar cells depletion in vsxKO larvae, with retinal precursors being rerouted toward photoreceptor or Müller glia fates.
evidence: Supported by histological analyses and marker expression data.

claim: Neural retina is properly specified and maintained in vsxKO zebrafish embryos.
source: Surprisingly, neural retina is properly specified and maintained in mutant embryos, which do not display microphthalmia.
evidence: Supported by histological and molecular analyses showing normal retinal specification.

claim: vsxKO zebrafish embryos do not display microphthalmia.
source: Surprisingly, neural retina is properly specified and maintained in mutant embryos, which do not display microphthalmia.
evidence: Supported by morphological observations and measurements.

claim: Important cis-regulatory remodelling occurs in vsxKO retinas during early specification.
source: We show that although important cis-regulatory remodelling occurs in vsxKO retinas during early specification, this has little impact at a transcriptomic level.
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq data showing differentially open chromatin regions.

claim: Cis-regulatory remodelling in vsxKO retinas has little impact at a transcriptomic level.
source: We show that although important cis-regulatory remodelling occurs in vsxKO retinas during early specification, this has little impact at a transcriptomic level.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data showing minimal transcriptional changes.

claim: Genetic redundancy is an important mechanism sustaining the integrity of the retinal specification network.
source: Our observations point to genetic redundancy as an important mechanism sustaining the integrity of the retinal specification network, and to Vsx genes regulatory weight varying substantially among vertebrate species.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that retinal specification proceeds normally despite vsx loss.

claim: Vsx genes regulatory weight varies substantially among vertebrate species.
source: Our observations point to genetic redundancy as an important mechanism sustaining the integrity of the retinal specification network, and to Vsx genes regulatory weight varying substantially among vertebrate species.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of zebrafish and mouse phenotypes.

claim: SIX3, PAX6, RAX, SOX2, VSX2, and OTX2 are transcriptional regulators recruited repeatedly for key developmental decisions at different stages of eye formation.
source: They comprise transcriptional regulators recruited repeatedly for key developmental decisions at different stages of eye formation, and which mutation in humans is often associated to severe ocular malformations: that is, microphthalmia, anophthalmia, and coloboma. This is the case for SIX3, PAX6, RAX, SOX2, VSX2, or OTX2 (Gregory-Evans et al., 2004; Gregory-Evans et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mutation of SIX3, PAX6, RAX, SOX2, VSX2, or OTX2 in humans is often associated with severe ocular malformations including microphthalmia, anophthalmia, and coloboma.
source: They comprise transcriptional regulators recruited repeatedly for key developmental decisions at different stages of eye formation, and which mutation in humans is often associated to severe ocular malformations: that is, microphthalmia, anophthalmia, and coloboma. This is the case for SIX3, PAX6, RAX, SOX2, VSX2, or OTX2 (Gregory-Evans et al., 2004; Gregory-Evans et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Vsx1 and Vsx2 control the development of visual circuits in vertebrate and invertebrate species.
source: Among the main regulators, the visual system homeobox transcription factors, Vsx1 and Vsx2, have been shown to control the development of visual circuits in vertebrate and invertebrate species (Burmeister et al., 1996; Erclik et al., 2008; Focareta et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Vsx2 was initially termed Chx10.
source: Vsx2, initially termed as Chx10, was the first gene of the family characterized in vertebrates (Liu et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Vsx2/Chx10 shows a conserved expression pattern across vertebrate species in the retina and in hindbrain and spinal cord interneurons.
source: Vsx2/Chx10 shows a conserved expression pattern across vertebrate species, both in the retina (i.e. early in all optic cup precursors, and later in retinal bipolar cells), as well as in hindbrain and spinal cord interneurons (Ferda Percin et al., 2000; Kimura et al., 2013; Liu et al., 1994; Passini et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A nonsense mutation in Vsx2 (Y176stop) is the molecular cause of the phenotype exhibited by the ocular retardation (or) mutant mice.
source: A nonsense mutation in Vsx2 (Y176stop) turned to be the molecular cause of the phenotype exhibited by the classical mutant mice ocular retardation (or), which displays microphthalmia and optic nerve aplasia (Burmeister et al., 1996; Truslove, 1962).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The ocular retardation (or) mutant mice display microphthalmia and optic nerve aplasia.
source: A nonsense mutation in Vsx2 (Y176stop) turned to be the molecular cause of the phenotype exhibited by the classical mutant mice ocular retardation (or), which displays microphthalmia and optic nerve aplasia (Burmeister et al., 1996; Truslove, 1962).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Vsx2 has an essential role in neuro-epithelial proliferation and bipolar cells differentiation.
source: The phenotypic analysis of or mutants, as well as the examination of human patients with hereditary microphthalmia, revealed an essential role for Vsx2 in neuro-epithelial proliferation and bipolar cells differentiation (BarYosef et al., 2004; Burmeister et al., 1996; Ferda Percin et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: During optic cup formation, Vsx2 is a key factor in the binary decision between neural retina and retinal-pigmented epithelium (RPE) lineages.
source: Subsequent studies indicated that, during optic cup formation, Vsx2 is a key factor in the binary decision between neural retina and retinal-pigmented epithelium (RPE) lineages.
evidence: Supported by citations to subsequent genetic studies.

claim: Vsx2 acts downstream of FGFs as a repressor of Mitf and Tfec genes and hence of the RPE identity.
source: Genetic studies in mice and chick revealed that Vsx2 acts, downstream of the neural retina inducing ligands (i.e. FGFs), as a repressor of Mitf and Tfec genes and hence of the RPE identity (Horsford et al., 2005; Nguyen and Arnheiter, 2000; Rowan et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Vsx1 was reported in several vertebrate species a few years after Vsx2 identification.
source: A few years after Vsx2 identification, a closely related paralog, Vsx1, was reported in several vertebrate species (Chen and Cepko, 2000; Chow et al., 2001; Levine et al., 1994; Passini et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Vsx1 and Vsx2 proteins have similar domains' architecture, including well-conserved paired-like homeodomain and CVC regulatory modules.
source: The proteins encoded by these paralogous genes have similar domains' architecture, including well-conserved paired-like homeodomain and CVC (Chx10/Vsx-1 and ceh-10) regulatory modules, and share biochemical properties, binding with high affinity to the same DNA sequence motif 'TAATTAGC' (Capowski et al., 2016; Dorval et al., 2005; Ferda Percin et al., 2000; Heon, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Vsx1 and Vsx2 proteins bind with high affinity to the same DNA sequence motif 'TAATTAGC'.
source: The proteins encoded by these paralogous genes have similar domains' architecture, including well-conserved paired-like homeodomain and CVC (Chx10/Vsx-1 and ceh-10) regulatory modules, and share biochemical properties, binding with high affinity to the same DNA sequence motif 'TAATTAGC' (Capowski et al., 2016; Dorval et al., 2005; Ferda Percin et al., 2000; Heon, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Vsx1 and Vsx2 display partially overlapping expression patterns in the retina.
source: Although both genes display partially overlapping expression patterns in the retina, Vsx2 precedes Vsx1 expression in undifferentiated progenitors in all vertebrate models analysed.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Vsx2 precedes Vsx1 expression in undifferentiated progenitors in all vertebrate models analysed.
source: Although both genes display partially overlapping expression patterns in the retina, Vsx2 precedes Vsx1 expression in undifferentiated progenitors in all vertebrate models analysed.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Once retinal precursors exit the cell cycle, Vsx1 and Vsx2 are expressed in complementary sets of differentiated bipolar cells.
source: Furthermore, once retinal precursors exit the cell cycle, they are expressed in complementary sets of differentiated bipolar cells.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In mice, Vsx1 is restricted to different types of ON and OFF cone bipolar cells.
source: Thus, Vsx1 is restricted to different types of ON and OFF cone bipolar cells in mice, and Vsx2 to S4 bipolar and Müller cells in zebrafish (Ohtoshi et al., 2004; Shi et al., 2011; Vitorino et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In zebrafish, Vsx2 is restricted to S4 bipolar and Müller cells.
source: Thus, Vsx1 is restricted to different types of ON and OFF cone bipolar cells in mice, and Vsx2 to S4 bipolar and Müller cells in zebrafish (Ohtoshi et al., 2004; Shi et al., 2011; Vitorino et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Vsx1 has a minor contribution to retinal specification in mammals.
source: In contrast to Vsx2, Vsx1 seems to have a minor contribution to retinal specification in mammals.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of early retinal phenotypes in Vsx1 mutant mice.

claim: A single case of sporadic microphthalmia has been associated with Vsx1 mutation in humans.
source: A single case of sporadic microphthalmia has been associated to Vsx1 mutation in humans (Matías-Pérez et al., 2018), and its mutation in mice does not affect early retinal development even in a Vsx2 mutant background (Chow et al., 2004; Clark et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Vsx1 mutation in mice does not affect early retinal development even in a Vsx2 mutant background.
source: A single case of sporadic microphthalmia has been associated to Vsx1 mutation in humans (Matías-Pérez et al., 2018), and its mutation in mice does not affect early retinal development even in a Vsx2 mutant background (Chow et al., 2004; Clark et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Vsx1 mutation has been linked to inherited corneal dystrophies in humans.
source: However, Vsx1 mutation has been linked to inherited corneal dystrophies in humans, and is associated to abnormal electroretinogram (ERGs) recordings either in mice or in patients (Chow et al., 2004; Heon, 2002; Mintz-Hittner et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Vsx1 mutation is associated with abnormal electroretinogram (ERG) recordings in mice and patients.
source: However, Vsx1 mutation has been linked to inherited corneal dystrophies in humans, and is associated to abnormal electroretinogram (ERGs) recordings either in mice or in patients (Chow et al., 2004; Heon, 2002; Mintz-Hittner et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Previous antisense oligonucleotides or morpholino studies in zebrafish showed that vsx2 knockdown results in microphthalmia and optic cup folding defects.
source: Previous antisense oligonucleotides or morpholino studies in zebrafish have shown that vsx2 knockdown results in microphthalmia and optic cup folding defects (Barabino et al., 1997; Clark et al., 2008; Gago-Rodrigues et al., 2015; Vitorino et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The findings from vsx2 morpholino studies in zebrafish have not been validated using knockout lines.
source: However, these findings have not been validated using knockout lines, neither the role of vsx1 and vsx2 in fate determination and bipolar cells differentiation has been sufficiently explored in teleost fish.
evidence: Stated as a gap in the literature.

claim: The role of vsx1 and vsx2 in fate determination and bipolar cells differentiation has not been sufficiently explored in teleost fish.
source: However, these findings have not been validated using knockout lines, neither the role of vsx1 and vsx2 in fate determination and bipolar cells differentiation has been sufficiently explored in teleost fish.
evidence: Stated as a gap in the literature.

claim: A 245 bp deletion was generated in vsx1 encompassing exon3, intron3, and exon4 of the gene (vsx1∆245).
source: We generated a 245 bp deletion in vsx1 encompassing exon3, intron3, and exon4 of the gene (vsx1∆245).
evidence: Described in methods and shown in Figure 1a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The vsx1∆245 mutation results in an in-frame deletion of 53 amino acids.
source: This mutation results in an in-frame deletion of 53 amino acids by the removal of 159 bp from exon3 (54 bp) and exon4 (105 bp; Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Described in text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: A 73 bp deletion was generated in vsx2 exon 3 (vsx2∆73).
source: In the case of vsx2, a 73 bp deletion was generated in exon 3 (vsx2∆73).
evidence: Described in methods and shown in Figure 1a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The vsx2∆73 mutation deletes 24 amino acids of the core DBD and generates a premature stop codon in that domain.
source: This mutation deletes 24 amino acids of the core DBD of the protein and generates a premature stop codon in that domain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Described in text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: No Vsx2 or Vsx1 proteins could be detected by western blot in 24hpf vsxKO samples.
source: Using Vsx1- and Vsx2-specific antibodies, we found that no Vsx2 or Vsx1 proteins could be detected by western blot in 24hpf vsxKO samples (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c, d).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c, d.

claim: No maternal Vsx1 protein was detected in early 1.5hpf wildtype embryos.
source: In addition, no maternal Vsx1 protein was detected in early 1.5hpf wildtype embryos (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Homozygous single mutants (vsx1∆245 or vsx2∆73) appeared normal in shape and size at 2-week post fertilization.
source: At 2-week post fertilization, no obvious macroscopic defects were observed in the visual system of either homozygous single mutants (i.e. vsx1∆245 or vsx2∆73) or homozygous double mutants vsx1∆245; vsx2∆73 (here termed vsxKO), which appeared normal in shape and size (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Figure 1—figure supplement 3a–d).
evidence: Supported by morphological observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3a–d.

claim: Homozygous double mutants vsx1∆245; vsx2∆73 (vsxKO) appeared normal in shape and size at 2-week post fertilization.
source: At 2-week post fertilization, no obvious macroscopic defects were observed in the visual system of either homozygous single mutants (i.e. vsx1∆245 or vsx2∆73) or homozygous double mutants vsx1∆245; vsx2∆73 (here termed vsxKO), which appeared normal in shape and size (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Figure 1—figure supplement 3a–d).
evidence: Supported by morphological observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3a–d.

claim: Homozygous single mutants and animals harboring a single wild type copy of either vsx1 or vsx2 reached adulthood and were fertile.
source: Homozygous single mutants, and even animals harboring a single wild type copy either of vsx1 (vsx1∆245+/-, vsx2∆73-/-) or vsx2 (vsx1∆245-/-; vsx2∆73+/-) reached adulthood and were fertile.
evidence: Observation from breeding experiments.

claim: Double mutant larvae (vsx1∆245 -/-; vsx2∆73 -/-) died at around 3-week post fertilization, with the exception of a single unfertile escaper reaching adulthood.
source: However, double mutant larvae (vsx1∆245 -/-; vsx2∆73 -/-) died at around 3-week post fertilization, with the exception of a single unfertile escaper reaching adulthood (1 out of 152 larvae raised).
evidence: Observation from breeding experiments.

claim: Histological sectioning of vsxKO mutant retinas at 48hpf showed a small delay in the formation of the inner plexiform layer (IPL).
source: Histological sectioning of mutant retinas at 48hpf showed a small delay in the formation of the inner plexiform layer (IPL), but no obvious macroscopic optic cup malformations when compared to WT (Figure 1b and f).
evidence: Supported by histological images shown in Figure 1b and f.

claim: At 48hpf, vsxKO mutant retinas showed no obvious macroscopic optic cup malformations when compared to WT.
source: Histological sectioning of mutant retinas at 48hpf showed a small delay in the formation of the inner plexiform layer (IPL), but no obvious macroscopic optic cup malformations when compared to WT (Figure 1b and f).
evidence: Supported by histological images shown in Figure 1b and f.

claim: At 72hpf, both the outer plexiform layer (OPL) and the IPL appeared less organized in the vsxKO double mutant retinas, showing discontinuities/fenestrae.
source: At 72hpf, both the outer plexiform layer (OPL) and the IPL appeared less organized in the double mutant retinas, which showed discontinuities/fenestrae (Figure 1c and g).
evidence: Supported by histological images shown in Figure 1c and g.

claim: At 6dpf, vsxKO double mutant larvae showed all the layers of a normal retina.
source: At 6dpf, double mutant larvae showed all the layers of a normal retina, but the thickness of the outer (ONL) and inner (INL) nuclear layers was significantly increased and reduced respectively, when compared to siblings (Figure 1d and h; Figure 1—figure supplement 3e, h, i).
evidence: Supported by histological images shown in Figure 1d and h.

claim: At 6dpf, the thickness of the outer nuclear layer (ONL) was significantly increased in vsxKO double mutants compared to siblings.
source: At 6dpf, double mutant larvae showed all the layers of a normal retina, but the thickness of the outer (ONL) and inner (INL) nuclear layers was significantly increased and reduced respectively, when compared to siblings (Figure 1d and h; Figure 1—figure supplement 3e, h, i).
evidence: Supported by histological images and quantification shown in Figure 1d, h and Figure 1—figure supplement 3i.

claim: At 6dpf, the thickness of the inner nuclear layer (INL) was significantly reduced in vsxKO double mutants compared to siblings.
source: At 6dpf, double mutant larvae showed all the layers of a normal retina, but the thickness of the outer (ONL) and inner (INL) nuclear layers was significantly increased and reduced respectively, when compared to siblings (Figure 1d and h; Figure 1—figure supplement 3e, h, i).
evidence: Supported by histological images and quantification shown in Figure 1d, h and Figure 1—figure supplement 3i.

claim: vsxKO fish presented expanded pigmentation in skin melanocytes even when exposed to bright light for 20 min.
source: In addition to retinal layer formation defects, vsxKO fish presented expanded pigmentation in skin melanocytes even when exposed to bright light for 20 min (Figure 1e and i; Figure 1—figure supplement 3a, d).
evidence: Supported by images shown in Figure 1e, i and Figure 1—figure supplement 3a, d.

claim: Expanded pigmentation in vsxKO fish is indicative of an impaired visual background adaptation (VBA) reflex.
source: This phenomenon is indicative of an impaired visual background adaptation (VBA) reflex, and is often associated with blindness in zebrafish (Fleisch and Neuhauss, 2006).
evidence: Inferred from established knowledge about VBA reflex and supported by citation.

claim: Zebrafish retina becomes fully functional at 5 dpf with the exception of late maturing rods.
source: Zebrafish retina becomes fully functional at 5 dpf with the exception of late maturing rods (Bilotta et al., 2001) and thus, the recorded field potentials were mainly contributed by cones.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: vsx2∆73 ERG response was similar to the WT recording.
source: We found that vsx2∆73 ERG response (green curve) was similar to the WT recording (blue curve).
evidence: Supported by ERG recordings shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Recordings in vsx1∆245 larvae showed a reduced b-wave compared to WT or vsx2∆73 larvae.
source: However, recordings in vsx1∆245 larvae showed a reduced b-wave compared to WT or vsx2∆73 larvae.
evidence: Supported by ERG recordings shown in Figure 2a, b.

claim: In 10 out of 36 double mutant larvae recorded, a reduced b-wave was observed compared to vsx1∆245 mutants.
source: From the 36 double mutant larvae recorded in total, 10 of them still showed a b-wave, though reduced in comparison to vsx1∆245 mutants, and much smaller than WT recordings.
evidence: Supported by ERG recordings shown in Figure 2a.

claim: In 26 out of 36 double mutant larvae recorded, only the negative a-wave but not the b-wave was detected.
source: Moreover, in the remaining 26 double mutants recorded only the negative a-wave but not the b-wave (gray curve) was detected, suggesting that bipolar cells differentiation and/or function might be compromised.
evidence: Supported by ERG recordings shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The b-wave is significantly decreased in both vsx1∆245 single and vsxKO double mutants in comparison to WT at all tested light intensities.
source: Statistical analysis of the average amplitude showed that the b-wave is significantly decreased in both vsx1∆245 single and vsxKO double mutants in comparison to WT at all tested light intensities (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of ERG data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The b-wave response amplitude in the vsxKO double mutant was significantly reduced compared to vsx1 single mutants.
source: In addition, the b-wave response amplitude in the double mutant was significantly reduced compared to vsx1 single mutants (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of ERG data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: A single wild type copy of vsx1 is sufficient to prevent VBA and ERG defects.
source: Interestingly, a single wild type copy of vsx1 is sufficient to prevent VBA and ERG defects, indicating that vsx2 loss of function can be compensated by vsx1.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of phenotypes in different genotypes.

claim: vsx2 loss of function can be compensated by vsx1.
source: Interestingly, a single wild type copy of vsx1 is sufficient to prevent VBA and ERG defects, indicating that vsx2 loss of function can be compensated by vsx1.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of phenotypes in different genotypes.

claim: Eye movement velocity was significantly reduced for vsx1 single and vsxKO double mutants when compared with vsx2∆73 larvae and WT controls in all OKR conditions tested.
source: In all conditions tested, we observed a significant reduction in eye velocity for vsx1 single and vsxKO double mutants when compared with vsx2∆73 larvae and WT controls (repeated measurement, ANOVA p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by OKR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: At 24 and 48hpf, no difference in the number of PH3+ cells were observed between WT and vsxKO retinas.
source: At 24 and 48hpf, no difference in the number of PH3 + cells were observed between WT and vsxKO retinas (Figure 3a, d and m; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by PH3 staining and quantification shown in Figure 3a, d, m and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: At 60hpf, vsxKO double mutant retinas showed a significant increase in PH3+ cells, particularly in the outer and peripheral regions.
source: However, at 60hpf, when the proliferation wave has largely finished in WT eyes, double mutant retinas continued to divide and showed a significant increase in PH3 + cells, particularly in the outer and peripheral regions (Figure 3b, e and m).
evidence: Supported by PH3 staining and quantification shown in Figure 3b, e, m.

claim: At 72hpf, PH3+ cells were only detected in the CMZ and no significant difference in the number of proliferative cells was detected between WT and vsxKO retinas.
source: Later on, at 72hpf, PH3 + cells were only detected in the CMZ and no significant difference in the number of proliferative cells was detected between WT and vsxKO retinas (Figure 3c, f and m).
evidence: Supported by PH3 staining and quantification shown in Figure 3c, f, m.

claim: At 60hpf, C3-positive cells (C3+) could be observed rarely in WT or vsxKO retinas.
source: At 60hpf, C3-positive cells (C3+) could be observed rarely in WT or vsxKO retinas (Figure 3g, j and n).
evidence: Supported by C3 staining and quantification shown in Figure 3g, j, n.

claim: At both 72 and 96hpf, a significant increase in the number of apoptotic C3+ cells were detected in vsxKO double mutants compared to WT.
source: However, at both 72 and 96hpf, a significant increase in the number of apoptotic C3 + cells were detected in double mutants compared to WT (Figure 3h, i, k and l).
evidence: Supported by C3 staining and quantification shown in Figure 3h, i, k, l, n.

claim: Apoptotic cells concentrated mainly in the INL layer of the vsxKO retina.
source: Apoptotic cells concentrated mainly in the INL layer of the retina (Figure 3k, l and n), suggesting that cell death within this layer may contribute to the decreased thickness observed in vsxKO retinas.
evidence: Supported by C3 staining shown in Figure 3k, l, n.

claim: A few apoptotic C3+ cells were observed in the ganglion cell layer (GCL) in vsxKO embryos.
source: We also observed a few apoptotic C3 + cells in the ganglion cell layer (GCL) in vsxKO embryos (Figure 3k and l) suggesting than the survival of these cells may be compromised.
evidence: Supported by C3 staining shown in Figure 3k, l.

claim: No obvious differences in retino-tectal projections were detected between WT and vsxKO double mutant larvae at 6dpf.
source: No obvious differences in retino-tectal projections were detected between WT and double mutant larvae, indicating that the RGCs are not affected in vsxKO retinas compared to control animals.
evidence: Supported by DiI/DiO tracing shown in Video 1.

claim: RGCs are not affected in vsxKO retinas compared to control animals.
source: No obvious differences in retino-tectal projections were detected between WT and double mutant larvae, indicating that the RGCs are not affected in vsxKO retinas compared to control animals.
evidence: Inferred from normal retino-tectal projections shown in Video 1.

claim: At 72hpf, prdm1a showed a mild downregulation in vsxKO embryos compared to wild type.
source: In this study, the comparative analysis of the transient marker prdm1a (Wilm and Solnica-Krezel, 2005) between wild type and vsxKO embryos revealed a mild downregulation in the mutants at 72 hpf (n=6) (Figure 4a and e), which is in agreement with the delayed differentiation of the photoreceptors we observed in vsxKO animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4a, e.

claim: A delayed differentiation of both cones and rods was observed in vsxKO double mutant embryos at 72 and 96hpf.
source: However, when we examined terminal differentiation markers for cones (Ab Zpr-1) and rods (Ab Zpr-3) at 72 and 96hpf, a delayed differentiation of both cell types was observed in double mutant embryos (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: At 6dpf, there is a significant increase of Zpr1 fluorescent intensity in vsxKO compared to WT retinas.
source: At 6dpf, there is a significant increase of Zpr1 fluorescent intensity in vsxKO compared to WT retinas (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c, f, g), but no major differences were observed in rod stain intensity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1j, m, n).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry and quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1c, f, g.

claim: No major differences in rod stain intensity were observed between WT and vsxKO at 6dpf.
source: At 6dpf, there is a significant increase of Zpr1 fluorescent intensity in vsxKO compared to WT retinas (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c, f, g), but no major differences were observed in rod stain intensity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1j, m, n).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry and quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1j, m, n.

claim: Cone cells are overrepresented in the ONL of the vsxKO double mutants.
source: This result suggests that PRs' differentiation program is delayed in the absence of vsx function and that cone cells are overrepresented in the ONL of the double mutants.
evidence: Inferred from increased Zpr1 staining in vsxKO retinas.

claim: At 48hpf, no changes in the expression of prox1 was detected between WT and vsxKO retinas.
source: At 48hpf, no changes in the expression of prox1 was detected between WT and vsxKO retinas (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a, e).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2a, e.

claim: At 72hpf, the nuclear distribution of prox1 in the INL is affected in vsxKO samples compared to WT retinas.
source: However, at 72hpf the nuclear distribution of prox1 in the INL is affected in vsxKO samples compared to WT retinas (Figure 4—figure supplement 2b, b', f, f') suggesting a lack of bipolar cells in vsxKO retinas.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2b, b', f, f'.

claim: At 72hpf, prkcbb expression is very reduced, if not absent, in the INL of vsxKO double mutant retinas compared to WT.
source: This observation was further confirmed by the fact that at 72hpf prkcbb expression is very reduced, if not absent, in the INL of double mutant retinas compared to WT (n=5) (Figure 4b and f).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4b, f.

claim: vsx genes are essential for bipolar cells specification in zebrafish.
source: These results are in agreement with our previous histological (i.e., reduced INL thickness; Figure 1—figure supplement 3) and electrophysiological (i.e. reduced b-wave, Figure 2) observations in vsxKO larvae, and confirms that vsx genes are essential for bipolar cells specification in zebrafish.
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of evidence including histology, ERG, and marker expression.

claim: The ACs differentiation wave progresses normally through the central retina in wild type and vsxKO embryos at 48 hpf.
source: Using a fluorescent probe against ptf1a, which is expressed transiently in all types of amacrine cells in the embryonic zebrafish retina (Jusuf and Harris, 2009), we could determine that the ACs differentiation wave progresses normally through the central retina in wild type and vsxKO embryos at 48 hpf (n=5) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2c, g).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2c, g.

claim: At 72 hpf, ptf1a expression appeared restricted to the most peripheral region and was expressed at similar levels in both wild type and vsxKO retinas.
source: Later in development, at 72 hpf, pft1a expression was no longer detected in the central retina and appeared restricted to the most peripheral region, being expressed at similar levels in both wild type and vsxKO retinas (n=10) (Figure 4c and g).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4c, g.

claim: The expression of the differentiated amacrine cell marker pax6 is not affected in vsxKO retinas compared to WT.
source: In addition, the expression of the differentiated amacrine cell marker pax6 (Hitchcock et al., 1996) is not affected in vsxKO retinas compared to WT (Figure 4—figure supplement 2d, h).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2d, h.

claim: vsx genes in zebrafish do not play a major role for amacrine cells specification.
source: These observations suggest that vsx genes in zebrafish do not play a major role for amacrine cells specification.
evidence: Inferred from normal expression of amacrine cell markers in vsxKO retinas.

claim: A clear increase in the expression of gfap was found in vsxKO retinas compared to WT.
source: We found a clear increase in the expression of gfap in vsxKO retinas compared to WT (n=5) (Figure 4d and h), suggesting that this cell type is overrepresented in vsxKO retinas, which may compensate for the reduction in bipolar cells observed in these animals.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4d, h.

claim: Müller glia cells are overrepresented in vsxKO retinas.
source: We found a clear increase in the expression of gfap in vsxKO retinas compared to WT (n=5) (Figure 4d and h), suggesting that this cell type is overrepresented in vsxKO retinas, which may compensate for the reduction in bipolar cells observed in these animals.
evidence: Inferred from increased gfap expression in vsxKO retinas.

claim: No significant differences in V2a or V2b spinal cord interneurons density was observed between WT and vsx1∆245-/-, vsx2∆73-/- mutant fish at 24hpf.
source: No significant differences in V2a or V2b spinal cord interneurons density was observed between WT (n=6) and vsx1∆245-/-, vsx2∆73-/- mutant fish (n=8) at 24hpf (Figure 4—figure supplement 3e).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization and quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: V2 motoneurons are properly specified in vsxKO animals.
source: These results suggest that V2 motoneurons are properly specified in vsxKO animals.
evidence: Inferred from normal density of V2a and V2b interneurons in vsxKO animals.

claim: The morphology and size of the optic cup appeared normal in vsxKO mutants at 24hpf.
source: In vsxKO mutants, the morphology and size of the optic cup, the precursors' proliferation rate, as well as the distribution and expression of RPE specification markers (i.e. tfec and bhlhe40) appeared normal at 24hpf, as determined by PH3 staining and ISH, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a‐g).
evidence: Supported by histology and marker expression shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The precursors' proliferation rate appeared normal in vsxKO mutants at 24hpf.
source: In vsxKO mutants, the morphology and size of the optic cup, the precursors' proliferation rate, as well as the distribution and expression of RPE specification markers (i.e. tfec and bhlhe40) appeared normal at 24hpf, as determined by PH3 staining and ISH, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a‐g).
evidence: Supported by PH3 staining shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a-c.

claim: The distribution and expression of RPE specification markers tfec and bhlhe40 appeared normal in vsxKO mutants at 24hpf.
source: In vsxKO mutants, the morphology and size of the optic cup, the precursors' proliferation rate, as well as the distribution and expression of RPE specification markers (i.e. tfec and bhlhe40) appeared normal at 24hpf, as determined by PH3 staining and ISH, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a‐g).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1d-g.

claim: The onset of retinal differentiation appeared slightly delayed in vsxKO mutants as determined by atoh7 ISH at 26 hpf.
source: The only parameter altered in vsxKO later in development is the onset of retinal differentiation, which appeared slightly delayed as determined by atoh7 ISH at 26 hpf (Figure 3—figure supplement 1h, i).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1h, i.

claim: ATAC-seq identified 1564 DNA regions with differential accessibility in vsxKO compared to WT at 18hpf.
source: This approach identified 1564 DNA regions with differential accessibility, most of them (1204) with a high fold change (i.e. log2 fold change > |1.5|).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 5a, b.

claim: 633 regions were more accessible in the vsxKO mutant with a log2 fold change >1.5.
source: They include 633 regions more accessible in the mutant with a log2 fold change >1.5; and 571 less accessible with a log2 fold change <–1.5 (Figure 5a and b; Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 5a, b.

claim: 571 regions were less accessible in the vsxKO mutant with a log2 fold change <–1.5.
source: They include 633 regions more accessible in the mutant with a log2 fold change >1.5; and 571 less accessible with a log2 fold change <–1.5 (Figure 5a and b; Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 5a, b.

claim: Enriched gene ontology terms for genes neighboring differentially opened regions revealed entries related to neuronal differentiation and eye development.
source: An analysis of enriched gene ontology terms for those genes (2219) neighboring the differentially opened regions revealed entries related to neuronal differentiation and eye development (Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by gene ontology analysis of ATAC-seq data.

claim: vsx genes mutation results in the deregulation of hundreds of cis-regulatory elements mainly associated to retinal genes.
source: This observation suggests that vsx genes mutation results in the deregulation of hundreds of cis-regulatory elements mainly associated to retinal genes.
evidence: Inferred from ATAC-seq data and gene ontology analysis.

claim: RNA-seq revealed expression changes in a relatively small gene set (1018) in vsxKO compared to WT at 18hpf.
source: In contrast, at a transcriptional level the comparative analysis of mutant and wild type samples by RNA-seq revealed expression changes only in a relatively small gene set (1018) (Figure 5c; Figure 5—source data 3).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: 41 genes were up-regulated (log2 fold change >1.5) in vsxKO compared to WT at 18hpf.
source: This collection comprised 41 up-regulated (log2 fold change >1.5) and 31 down-regulated (log2 Fold change <–1.5) genes, with only 3 up-regulated (vsx1, znf1109, and znf1102) and one down-regulated transcription factor (znf1091) above the threshold (log2 fold change > |1.5|) (Figure 5c).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: 31 genes were down-regulated (log2 fold change <–1.5) in vsxKO compared to WT at 18hpf.
source: This collection comprised 41 up-regulated (log2 fold change >1.5) and 31 down-regulated (log2 Fold change <–1.5) genes, with only 3 up-regulated (vsx1, znf1109, and znf1102) and one down-regulated transcription factor (znf1091) above the threshold (log2 fold change > |1.5|) (Figure 5c).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Only 3 up-regulated transcription factors (vsx1, znf1109, and znf1102) were above the threshold (log2 fold change > |1.5|) in vsxKO compared to WT.
source: This collection comprised 41 up-regulated (log2 fold change >1.5) and 31 down-regulated (log2 Fold change <–1.5) genes, with only 3 up-regulated (vsx1, znf1109, and znf1102) and one down-regulated transcription factor (znf1091) above the threshold (log2 fold change > |1.5|) (Figure 5c).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: One down-regulated transcription factor (znf1091) was above the threshold (log2 fold change > |1.5|) in vsxKO compared to WT.
source: This collection comprised 41 up-regulated (log2 fold change >1.5) and 31 down-regulated (log2 Fold change <–1.5) genes, with only 3 up-regulated (vsx1, znf1109, and znf1102) and one down-regulated transcription factor (znf1091) above the threshold (log2 fold change > |1.5|) (Figure 5c).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Among the 2219 genes neighboring differentially open chromatin regions, only 5% (119) were associated with differentially expressed genes.
source: In fact, among the 2219 genes neighboring differentially open chromatin regions, only 5% (119) were associated to differentially expressed genes (Figure 5d).
evidence: Supported by comparison of ATAC-seq and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: In vsxKO embryos, significant expression changes could be detected only for rx2 and lhx2b among core components of the neural retina GRN at 19 hpf.
source: Interestingly, in vsxKO embryos significant expression changes could be detected only for rx2 and lhx2b (although below the threshold log2 fold change > |1.5|).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: The transcripts of vsx1 were significantly upregulated in vsxKO mutant embryos at optic cup stages.
source: In addition, the transcripts of the mutated genes vsx1 and vsx2 were significantly upregulated and downregulated respectively in mutant embryos at optic cup stages, as determined by qPCR at 19hpf (Figure 5e) and confirmed by ISH at 24hpf (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by qPCR and ISH data shown in Figure 5e and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The transcripts of vsx2 were significantly downregulated in vsxKO mutant embryos at optic cup stages.
source: In addition, the transcripts of the mutated genes vsx1 and vsx2 were significantly upregulated and downregulated respectively in mutant embryos at optic cup stages, as determined by qPCR at 19hpf (Figure 5e) and confirmed by ISH at 24hpf (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by qPCR and ISH data shown in Figure 5e and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The general architecture of the retinal GRN was not significantly altered upon vsx genes mutation.
source: Taken together, these analyses suggest that the general architecture of the retinal GRN was not significantly altered upon vsx genes mutation.
evidence: Inferred from RNA-seq and qPCR data showing minimal changes in core retinal genes.

claim: Principal components analysis (PCA) of wild type, morphant and double mutant datasets revealed a very different regulatory response between mutant and morphant samples.
source: Principal components analysis (PCA) of wild type, morphant and double mutant datasets revealed a very different regulatory response between mutant and morphant samples (Figure 5—figure supplement 2b; Figure 5—source data 4).
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2b.

claim: Core components of the retinal network such as rx3, rx1, six3b, vax2, and lhx2b appeared upregulated in the vsx2 morphants.
source: This differential behavior was evident when core components of the eye specification gene regulatory networks were examined: whereas mild transcriptional differences were detected for rx2 and lhx2b in the mutants (Figure 5; Figure 5—figure supplement 2c), core components of the retinal network such as rx3, rx1, six3b, vax2, and lhx2b appeared upregulated in the morphants (Figure 5—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2c.

claim: vsx2 expression appeared strongly downregulated in vsxKO mutants but strongly upregulated in vsx2 morphants.
source: Particularly different was the expression of vsx2 itself, which appeared strongly downregulated in vsxKO mutants, but strongly upregulated in vsx2 morphants (Figure 5—figure supplement 2d, f).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2d, f.

claim: The dysregulation of the retinal network induced by the morpholinos is behind the early microphthalmia observed in the vsx2 morphants.
source: These results suggest that the dysregulation of the retinal network induced by the morpholinos (i.e. may be through compensatory mechanisms operating at the RNA level) is behind the early microphthalmia observed in the vsx2 morphants.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of transcriptomes and phenotypes between morphants and mutants.

claim: The initial specification of the organ appeared normal in medaka vsx1/vsx2.1 double mutant embryos at 4dpf.
source: Interestingly, although the initial specification of the organ appeared normal also in medaka double mutant embryos at 4dpf, INL differentiation and eye growth was impaired at later stages in those animals (Figure 5—figure supplement 3b–e).
evidence: Supported by histological images shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3b-e.

claim: INL differentiation and eye growth was impaired at later stages in medaka vsx1/vsx2.1 double mutant animals.
source: Interestingly, although the initial specification of the organ appeared normal also in medaka double mutant embryos at 4dpf, INL differentiation and eye growth was impaired at later stages in those animals (Figure 5—figure supplement 3b–e).
evidence: Supported by histological images shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3b-e.

claim: The hierarchic weight of Vsx genes within the eye GRNs varies considerably across vertebrate species.
source: In summary, whereas our work shows a conserved role for Vsx genes during bipolar cell differentiation, also indicates that their hierarchic weight within the eye GRNs varies considerably across vertebrate species.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of phenotypes in zebrafish, medaka, and mouse.

claim: Vsx genes have a conserved role during bipolar cell differentiation across vertebrate species.
source: In summary, whereas our work shows a conserved role for Vsx genes during bipolar cell differentiation, also indicates that their hierarchic weight within the eye GRNs varies considerably across vertebrate species.
evidence: Supported by data showing bipolar cell defects in zebrafish vsxKO mutants.

claim: Vsx activity is essential for bipolar cells differentiation in teleost fish.
source: Here, we show that Vsx activity is essential for bipolar cells differentiation in teleost fish, indicating a broadly conserved role for these genes across vertebrates.
evidence: Supported by data showing bipolar cell depletion in vsxKO zebrafish.

claim: The genetic program controlling bipolars specification was inherited from a common vertebrate ancestor.
source: This observation suggests that the genetic program controlling bipolars specification was inherited from a common vertebrate ancestor.
evidence: Inferred from conserved role of Vsx genes in bipolar cell differentiation across vertebrates.

claim: The function for Vsx homeobox genes in the specification of visual interneurons may be a common theme in all metazoans.
source: The fact that Vsx homologous genes are also expressed in the visual-system of the invertebrates Drosophila and Cuttlefish (Sepia officinalis) further suggests that the function for these homeobox genes in the specification of visual interneurons may be a common theme in all metazoans (Erclik et al., 2008; Focareta et al., 2014).
evidence: Inferred from expression of Vsx homologs in invertebrate visual systems and supported by citations.

claim: Unable to acquire the bipolar fate, retinal precursors in vsxKO follow alternative differentiation trajectories such as undergoing apoptosis, extending their proliferative phase, or differentiating as photoreceptors or Müller glia cells.
source: We show that, unable to acquire the bipolar fate, retinal precursors follow alternative differentiation trajectories such as undergoing apoptosis, extending their proliferative phase, or differentiating as photoreceptors or Müller glia cells.
evidence: Supported by data on proliferation, apoptosis, and cell fate markers in vsxKO retinas.

claim: A detour toward photoreceptors fate in zebrafish vsxKO is in agreement with previous studies in mice showing that the Blimp1/Vsx2 antagonism controls the balance between rods and bipolar cells.
source: A detour toward photoreceptors fate in zebrafish is in agreement with previous studies in mice showing that the Blimp1/Vsx2 antagonism controls the balance between rods and bipolar cells (Brzezinski et al., 2010; Goodson et al., 2020; Katoh et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research in mice.

claim: In vsxKO retinas, a noticeable delay in the onset of cones and rods terminal differentiation markers was observed.
source: Interestingly, in vsxKO retinas we observed a noticeable delay in the onset of cones and rods terminal differentiation markers, zpr-1 and zpr-3 respectively, indicating that Vsx activity is not only required for correct fate specification, but also to determine the timing of the differentiation sequence, in agreement with previous data in mice (Rutherford et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data and citation to prior research.

claim: Vsx activity is required to determine the timing of the differentiation sequence.
source: Interestingly, in vsxKO retinas we observed a noticeable delay in the onset of cones and rods terminal differentiation markers, zpr-1 and zpr-3 respectively, indicating that Vsx activity is not only required for correct fate specification, but also to determine the timing of the differentiation sequence, in agreement with previous data in mice (Rutherford et al., 2004).
evidence: Inferred from delayed photoreceptor differentiation in vsxKO retinas and supported by citation.

claim: Both glial and bipolars cells are late-born retinal types deriving from a common pool of precursors with restricted developmental potential.
source: Both glial and bipolars cells are late-born retinal types deriving from a common pool of precursors with restricted developmental potential (Bassett and Wallace, 2012; Hatakeyama et al., 2001; Rowan and Cepko, 2004; Satow et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In mice, a significant increase in Müller glia cells has not been reported in experiments genetically interfering with vsx either postnatally or specifically in bipolar cells.
source: In mice, however, a significant increase in Müller glia cells has not been reported in experiments genetically interfering with vsx either postnatally (Goodson et al., 2020; Livne-Bar et al., 2006) or specifically in bipolar cells (Norrie et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The apparent discrepancy in Müller glia increase between zebrafish and mice might indicate some variations in the cell fate specification mechanisms among vertebrate species.
source: This apparent discrepancy might indicate some variations in the cell fate specification mechanisms among vertebrate species.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of differences between zebrafish and mouse phenotypes.

claim: The increase in Müller glia may have been overlooked in previous mouse studies due to the small size of the Müller glia cell population.
source: Alternatively, the increase may have been overlooked in previous studies due to the small size of the Müller glia cell population. The fact that a trend toward an increase in Müller glia has been reported (Livne-Bar et al., 2006) may support this second possibility.
evidence: Speculative interpretation supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Neuro-retinal identity seemed perfectly maintained in vsxKO double mutant animals.
source: More importantly, neuro-retinal identity seemed perfectly maintained in double mutant animals, and we did not detect any trans-differentiation of the retina into pigmented cells.
evidence: Supported by marker expression and histological data.

claim: No trans-differentiation of the retina into pigmented cells was detected in vsxKO double mutant animals.
source: More importantly, neuro-retinal identity seemed perfectly maintained in double mutant animals, and we did not detect any trans-differentiation of the retina into pigmented cells.
evidence: Supported by marker expression and histological data.

claim: Vsx genes do not play an early role in the establishment and maintenance of the neural retina identity in zebrafish.
source: This finding, which is in contrast with the microphthalmia and the neural retina specification defects observed in mice (Burmeister et al., 1996; Horsford et al., 2005; Rowan et al., 2004), may indicate that Vsx genes do not play an early role in the establishment and maintenance of the neural retina identity in zebrafish.
evidence: Inferred from normal retinal specification in vsxKO zebrafish.

claim: A potential rescue by maternally provided vsx genes is an unlikely possibility as both transcripts are not detectable before zygotic genome activation.
source: Although a potential rescue by maternally provided vsx genes could be hypothesized as an explanation for normal specification of the retina, this is an unlikely possibility as both transcripts are not detectable before zygotic genome activation (White et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research on transcript detection.

claim: A poor resemblance between morpholino-induced and mutant phenotypes has been previously described in zebrafish, with many mutations lacking observable phenotypes.
source: A poor resemblance between morpholino-induced and mutant phenotypes has been previously described in zebrafish, with many mutations lacking observable phenotypes (Kok et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Genetic compensation and transcriptional adaptation have been identified as molecular mechanisms accounting for genetic robustness in zebrafish mutations.
source: Genetic compensation and, in particular, transcriptional adaptation (i.e. up-regulation of genes displaying sequence similarity) has been identified as the molecular mechanism accounting for genetic robustness in a number of these mutations (El-Brolosy et al., 2019; Rossi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The comparative transcriptomic analysis of vsxKO vs WT embryos does not support genetic compensation acting as a relevant mechanism at optic cup stages.
source: However, our comparative transcriptomic analysis of vsxKO vs WT embryos does not support genetic compensation acting as a relevant mechanism at optic cup stages.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data showing minimal transcriptional changes.

claim: The regulatory networks involved in the specification of the zebrafish eye are remarkably robust.
source: Our previous analysis of transcriptome dynamics and chromatin accessibility in segregating NR/RPE populations indicated that the regulatory networks involved in the specification of the zebrafish eye are remarkably robust (Buono et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The consensus motif 5'-TAATT-3' is central to the neural retina cis-regulatory logic and is shared by many homeodomain TFs co-expressed during retinal specification.
source: In that study, we showed that the consensus motif 5'-TAATT-3', which is central to the neural retina cis-regulatory logic, is shared by many homeodomain TFs co-expressed during retinal specification; including not only vsx1 and vsx2, but also rx1, rx2, rx3, lhx2b, lhx9, hmx1, and hmx4.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Homeodomain TFs co-expressed during retinal specification may co-regulate the same genes and cooperate within the same cis-regulatory modules.
source: Moreover, we show evidence that these TFs may co-regulate the same genes and cooperate within the same cis-regulatory modules (Buono et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Gene redundancy appears as a more parsimonious explanation for the absence of an early phenotype in vsxKO embryos.
source: According to these observations, gene redundancy appears as a more parsimonious explanation for the absence of an early phenotype in vsxKO embryos.
evidence: Inferred from the robustness of the retinal specification network and the lack of early phenotype.

claim: Other mutations in genes encoding for TFs targeting the motif 5'-TAATT-3', such as rx2 in medaka or lhx2 in zebrafish, do not compromise the identity of the neural retina tissue.
source: (i) Other mutations in genes encoding for TFs targeting the motif 5'-TAATT-3', such as rx2 in medaka (Reinhardt et al., 2015) or lhx2 in zebrafish (Seth et al., 2006) do not compromise the identity of the neural retina tissue either.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Even in vsx1/vsx2 double mutant mice, the central retina keeps the potential for differentiation into several neuronal types.
source: (ii) Even in vsx1/vsx2 double mutant mice, the central retina keeps the potential for differentiation into several neuronal types, indicating that other genes must cooperate in the specification of this tissue (Clark et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: In Vsx2 mutant mice, neural retinal identity defects and microphthalmia (but not bipolar cells differentiation) can be partially restored by simply deleting a cell cycle gene.
source: In line with this, in Vsx2 mutant mice has been shown that neural retinal identity defects and microphthalmia (but not bipolar cells differentiation) can be partially restored by simply deleting a cell cycle gene (Green et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The mutation of the paralogs vsx1 and vsx2.2 results in severe microphthalmia in medaka larvae.
source: (iii) Finally, here we show that the mutation of the paralogs vsx1 and vsx2.2 results in severe microphthalmia in medaka larvae.
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The finding that vsx1/vsx2.2 mutation results in microphthalmia in medaka confirms a variable role across species for Vsx genes in the specification and maintenance of the neural retina domain in vertebrates.
source: This finding confirms a variable role across species for Vsx genes in the specification and maintenance of the neural retina domain in vertebrates.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of phenotypes in zebrafish, medaka, and mouse.
